extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning formal and informal logic, philosophy, and critical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, evaluate, and avoid common formal and informal logical fallacies in argumentative prose; includes criteria for diagnosing equivocation, begging the question, irrelevant conclusions, composition/division errors, and related defects in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of terms / Equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of error when a word or phrase has different senses in different parts of an argument so that premises appear to support a conclusion only by shifting meaning (equivocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect whether key terms retain a single meaning throughout the argument. Examples: Berkeley's argument (confounding sameness numero with sameness specie); Playfair's vis viva dispute (the word 'force' used for different effects). Check for tacit shifts in sense between premises and conclusion; if found, the inference is invalid. Where ambiguity exists, clarify definitions or restate premises with consistent senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confounding identity (sameness numero) with resemblance (sameness specie)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating two occurrences as the identical individual rather than as distinct occurrences of the same type or kind (exact resemblance), leading to illicit inferences about persistence or ontological status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When someone says 'I have the same thought today that I had yesterday,' interpret whether they mean the identical mental item or an exactly similar one. Avoid inferring continued existence of an item outside of a mind from such locutions. Ask whether 'same' is being used numerically (the selfsame instance) or speciously (same sort).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing infinite divisibility with infinite duration/extent
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistaking that because a quantity can be subdivided without end, the total quantity or duration must itself be infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Achilles and the Tortoise example: infinite divisibility of time or distance (arbitrarily many subdivisions) does not imply the whole interval is infinite. Clarify whether 'ever' or 'forever' in an argument refers to 'for any number of subdivisions' (divisibility) or 'for any length of time' (unbounded duration). Insist on precise quantification when infinities or limits are invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Composition and Division
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing to the whole a property that holds only of the parts (composition), or attributing to parts a property that holds only of the whole (division), often via a shift between collective and distributive senses of a term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the distributive/collective status of the middle term in each premise and in the conclusion. Examples: inferring 'all great men could have been dispensed with' from premises about individual great men being replaceable; lottery arguments conflating 'no uncommon occurrence to someone' with 'no uncommon occurrence to a particular individual.' Ensure that premises and conclusion use the term in the same (collective or distributive) sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitio Principii (Begging the Question), including Reasoning in a Circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a premise that is identical with or depends upon the conclusion to be proved, or proving propositions reciprocally from one another so that the chain of inference has no independent foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the premise either appears manifestly the same as the conclusion, is actually proved from the conclusion, or would naturally be proved from the conclusion. Disguises include: expressing the same proposition in abstract vs. concrete terms, using mutually coherent but unsupported premises, and circular reciprocal proofs. A practical test: challenge the reasoner to supply independent proof of the premises — if they appeal back to the conclusion, the reasoning is circular. Examples: attempts to prove every particle gravitates equally by reasoning that presupposes that fact; ethical systems that assume the sage must be happy and so beg the question about the summum bonum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguises of Petitio: abstract 'nature'/'essence' language and indefeasible generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using grand abstract terms (e.g., 'nature', 'essence') or selecting certain properties as the 'essence' of a thing in order to immunize them from counter-evidence and thereby smuggle in the conclusion as a premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious when a writer appeals to 'nature' or 'essence' to settle a question. Ask for empirical or independent reasons rather than accepting that a selected property is ipso facto decisive. Examples: Aristotle's use of 'nature' to dismiss a void, or scholastic claims that 'the essence of the mind is to think' used to infer perpetual thought. Rephrase such claims concretely and test whether they actually provide independent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-begging appellatives (loaded labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing laudatory or vituperative labels whose connotation prejudges the issue (naming that asserts the very point in dispute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when words with strong positive or negative connotations are used as if they were arguments (e.g., calling an innovation 'an innovation' with the intended pejorative force). Insist on arguments and evidence rather than relying on emotive or loaded terminology. Replace appellative labels with neutral descriptions and evaluate the neutral claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paronymous-terms fallacy (confusing related word-forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deriving a fallacious inference from similarity of word-forms (paronyms) that have different meanings or implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: confusion between cupiditas and cupidus. Check whether derivations or transformations between related terms actually preserve the relevant meaning. Avoid inferring properties merely from morphological or etymological similarity; require semantic justification for any step that relies on a word-form relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoratio Elenchi (Irrelevant Conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting or proving a proposition different from the one that ought to be established, thereby winning assent or emotional response while leaving the original question unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the conclusion actually answers the question posed. Beware tactics that prove a related but distinct claim (e.g., proving a fraud is atrocious rather than proving the accused committed that fraud). Look for substitution of particular for universal (or vice versa), or introduction of a different proposition with similar rhetorical effect. Guard against appeals to emotion or prejudice that accomplish 'practical' persuasion without addressing the precise issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper appeal to passions and extraneous matters (appeal to emotions as substitute for proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using emotion, ridicule, or irrelevant associative imagery to produce the practical effect of refutation while avoiding the logical burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: making an audience laugh to neutralize a defense; labeling an accused person a 'rogue' to extinguish relevant mitigating circumstances. Insist on substantive refutation of the specific claim rather than rhetorical moves that provoke sentiment. Ask: does the response engage with the asserted reasons or merely provoke an emotional reaction?

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking mutual coherence for independent truth (coherence without foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting as true a system of mutually supporting propositions because they form a neat concatenation, when none have independent external support — i.e., trusting internal consistency as if it were sufficient for truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between internal coherence and independent justification. Even a strongly coherent system can be false if its foundational premises lack support. When a doctrine seems to 'hold together' nicely, search for a non-circular grounding or independent evidence. Be alert to the 'safety' of a strong chain that has no point of support beyond itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding a priori construction of methods; ground principles of evidence empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of evidence and theories of method should not be constructed purely a priori but learned by observing the actual operation of the rational faculty and scientific practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the moral sciences (and more generally), derive rules of method by examining successful historical practice and observed results rather than by pure deduction from supposed first principles. The earlier achievements of science often preceded formal methods; methods should be induced from what works, and we should not ascribe greater certainty to such inductively grounded conjectures than the empirical basis warrants.
